title: Design Search Autocomplete
subtitle: Watch each keystroke become a sub-100 ms suggestion list, and see how the index behind it is built and refreshed.
learn: Why a trie (prefix tree) fits prefix lookups, and why walking it per request is still too slow
How storing the top-k suggestions on every prefix node turns a query into one lookup
How search logs flow through a queue and batch job to rebuild the index
Why edge caching works so well for short prefixes, and what it costs in freshness
How to split a ~100 ms latency budget across client, network, edge and server

steps.title: Suggest while they type
steps.body: A user types 'wea' and expects 'weather', 'weather tomorrow' and 'wearable tech' to appear before they finish the next letter. Assume 5 billion searches a day and about 4 suggestion requests per search once the client waits for a short typing pause. That is roughly 20 billion requests a day, about 230k per second on average and perhaps 700k at peak. Each answer must feel instant, so we aim for under 100 ms, measured from the request being sent to the list being drawn.
steps.idea: Autocomplete is a read-heavy, latency-critical lookup: huge request volume, tiny responses, strict deadline.
steps.caption: Every pause in typing sends a prefix to the system.

steps.title: A trie finds prefixes
steps.body: A trie stores strings one character per level, so every word sharing 'wea' hangs below the same path w-e-a. Finding the node for a prefix takes time proportional to the prefix length, not the number of stored queries. That is exactly the shape of our question. But the node only tells us where the matches start. Collecting every completion beneath 'w' would mean scanning millions of descendants.
steps.idea: A trie makes 'find everything starting with X' cheap to locate, but expensive to enumerate and rank.
steps.caption: The index is a trie, but we cannot scan subtrees per request.

steps.title: Precompute top-k per prefix
steps.body: The fix is to do the ranking ahead of time. Every trie node stores its top k completions, with k around 10, already sorted by popularity score. A request now walks at most a few dozen characters and returns the list sitting on that node, with no subtree scan and no sorting. The price is memory and build time: each popular query is copied into the lists of all its prefixes. As a rule of thumb that is still only a few GB per shard, so it fits in RAM. In practice the same prefix-to-list idea can live in a compressed trie or a plain key-value map; the trie is the clearest way to picture it.
steps.idea: Trade space and offline work for speed: store the answer on each prefix so the read path is one lookup.
steps.caption: Each prefix node already holds its ranked suggestions.

steps.title: Most requests end at the edge
steps.body: The client sends a prefix such as 'wea' after a 100 to 150 ms typing pause, cancelling any older in-flight request. The request goes to an edge cache near the user. Short prefixes are shared by millions of people, so the same URL (for example /suggest?q=wea) is asked again and again. The cache key is the normalized prefix plus language/locale, and personalization would lower the hit rate. With a TTL of a few minutes, assume about 90% as a rule of thumb for a non-personalized, short-TTL setup; this lesson uses 90% for the numbers. A hit costs only one short network hop.
steps.idea: Because short prefixes are asked by everyone, caching the response at the edge absorbs most of the load.
steps.caption: Edge cache answers a popular prefix directly.

steps.title: A miss goes to the index
steps.body: Long or rare prefixes like 'weather in lisb' are unlikely to be in the edge cache yet, so the edge forwards them to the suggest service. The service looks up the prefix in the in-memory index and returns the stored list. Because there is no scan, server time is around 1 to 5 ms. The edge stores the response, with a short TTL since few people will repeat it, so the next person typing the same prefix gets a hit. Only the remaining ~10% of traffic, about 70k per second of the 700k total at peak, reaches this tier.
steps.idea: The origin sees only misses, and each miss is a single in-memory lookup.
steps.caption: Miss: edge asks the service, service reads the index.

steps.title: Collect what people search
steps.body: Suggestions are only as good as the popularity data behind them. When a user actually submits a search, the search backend (or a small client beacon) appends an event to a log stream, off the critical path so a slow log never slows suggestions. We draw it from the suggest tier to keep the picture small. We log only completed searches, not every keystroke, which is both less noise and less volume. Raw logs also need cleaning later: bots, abuse and private queries must not become suggestions.
steps.idea: Feed the index from completed searches, written asynchronously so reads stay fast.
steps.caption: Submitted searches are logged to a stream.

steps.title: Aggregate and rebuild
steps.body: A batch job reads the stream, filters spam and sensitive terms, drops queries searched by only a handful of distinct users so rare private strings never surface, and counts each query over a window, often with a recency weighting so fresh interest counts more than old. It writes the counts to storage, then builds a new trie with top-k lists per node. The finished index is shipped to the serving machines as a whole new version. A rebuild every hour or so is common, with the heavy work done offline on separate machines.
steps.idea: Ranking is computed offline in batches, so the serving path never does aggregation.
steps.caption: Worker counts queries and builds a fresh index.

steps.title: Freshness versus speed
steps.body: A breaking-news term can surge in minutes, yet an hourly rebuild plus a few minutes of edge TTL means it can appear up to an hour or more late (the average lag is shorter, but the worst case is what users notice). Teams close the gap with a small separate 'trending' list updated every minute or so from a stream counter, and merge it into results at request time, which brings the visible age for spikes down to about 5 minutes while the main index stays hourly. Swapping in a new index is done by loading the new version beside the old one and switching atomically, so readers never see a half-built trie.
steps.idea: Batch rebuilds give stable, cheap ranking; a small fast side-channel handles breaking trends.
steps.caption: Stale by design: fresher data costs more work.

steps.title: Spend the 100 ms
steps.body: Here is a defensible budget for a miss. The 100 ms budget is measured from when the request is sent to when the list is drawn. The debounce delay comes on top, which is why many clients use a short pause (50 to 150 ms) or skip it for the first characters. Then roughly 30 ms round trip to the edge, 20 ms round trip from edge to origin, 2 to 5 ms for the lookup, and a few ms to render the list. An edge hit skips the origin trip entirely. Network distance is the biggest term, which is why the edge cache matters more than a faster trie.
steps.idea: Latency is dominated by distance; the index lookup is the cheap part.
steps.caption: Edge hit about 35 ms, full miss about 60 ms.

steps.title: The whole design
steps.body: Reads: debounce on the client, answer from the edge when possible, otherwise do one lookup of a precomputed top-k list in a memory-resident trie. Writes: log completed searches to a stream, aggregate and filter in batches, build a new index, and swap it in atomically. Scaling the index means sharding by prefix range and replicating each shard for load and failure. The key move is shifting all expensive work from request time to build time.
steps.idea: Make reads trivial by precomputing answers, and refresh them on a schedule you can afford.
steps.caption: Fast read path on top, slow build path below.

quiz.q: Why store the top-k list on every trie node instead of computing it when a request arrives?
options: It lets the trie use less memory
Finding all completions under a short prefix means scanning a huge subtree, which is far too slow per request
Tries cannot be traversed at request time
It removes the need to log searches
quiz.why: A prefix like 'w' has millions of descendants. Precomputing the ranked list trades memory and build time for a constant-time read.

quiz.q: Edge hit rate for short prefixes is much higher than for long ones. What is the best explanation?
options: Edge servers have more memory for short strings
Long prefixes are blocked by CDNs
Short prefixes are never updated
Short prefixes are shared by many users, so the same request repeats often
quiz.why: Few distinct short prefixes exist and everyone types them, so the same cache key is requested constantly. Long prefixes are far more varied.

quiz.q: A new celebrity name starts trending, but suggestions miss it for over an hour. Which change best targets this without rebuilding the whole index more often?
options: Add more edge locations
Raise k from 10 to 100
Add a small, frequently updated trending list merged at request time
Store the trie on disk instead of memory
quiz.why: The delay comes from batch rebuild interval and cache TTL. A small fast-updating side list covers spikes cheaply while the big index stays batch-built.

quiz.q: Why is the search event written to the log stream asynchronously?
options: So the suggestion response does not wait on logging, and a slow or failing log cannot hurt latency
Because queues guarantee ranking order
Because the trie requires a write on every read
To reduce the edge hit rate
quiz.why: Logging is not needed to answer the user. Keeping it off the critical path protects the latency budget.

quiz.q: The p99 latency is 300 ms for users far from your region, while lookup time is 3 ms. What is the most effective fix?
options: Serve cached suggestions from edges near those users
Replace the trie with a faster data structure
Increase k so fewer requests are needed
Rebuild the index more often
quiz.why: Time is dominated by network distance, not the lookup. Moving answers closer to users removes the biggest term.

cheatsheet.def: A tree where each edge is a character, so strings sharing a prefix share a path. Finding a prefix costs time proportional to its length.
Each trie node stores its k best completions (k around 10), ranked in advance, so a request needs no subtree scan or sort.
The client waits a short pause (about 100 to 150 ms) after the last keystroke before sending, and cancels stale requests, cutting traffic a lot.
Short prefixes repeat across users, so caching responses near users with a TTL of minutes absorbs most traffic. Cost: results lag the index.
Logs, aggregation, filtering and trie construction run in batches off the serving path, then ship as a new version swapped in atomically.
Split the index by prefix range (for example a-c, d-f) across machines, with replicas for load and failover. Watch for skewed popular ranges.
Index age plus cache TTL is how stale suggestions can be. Fix spikes with a small fast trending list rather than constant full rebuilds.
Split a target (about 100 ms) across stages. Network distance usually dominates; the in-memory lookup is only a few ms.

lab.prompt: Design autocomplete for a search engine with 5 billion searches a day. Suggestions must appear within 100 ms of the request being sent (after a short client-side debounce), rank by popularity, and reflect new trends reasonably quickly. Sketch the read path, the build path, and how you would shard and refresh the index.
requirements: Return up to 10 ranked suggestions for any prefix
End-to-end p95 latency under 100 ms at about 700k requests per second peak
Rank by popularity with some recency weighting
Keep offensive, private and bot-generated queries out of suggestions
Surface a new trending term within roughly 15 minutes
Survive the loss of a serving machine or a failed index build
hints: Start from the read path and ask what answer could be precomputed so a request is one lookup.
Estimate cache hit rate for short prefixes first; it decides how big the origin tier must be.
Treat the build as a separate batch pipeline fed by completed searches, not keystrokes.
Think about how you would roll out a new index version safely and roll it back.
Shard by prefix range, but check how uneven the traffic across ranges would be.
checklist: Client debounces and cancels stale requests
Edge cache with sensible TTL for popular prefixes
Trie with precomputed top-k per node, held in memory
Async log stream plus batch aggregation and filtering
Atomic index swap and a plan for stale data
Sharding and replication plan, with failure behavior
Latency budget that adds up to under 100 ms
